summary:
On the way to Mars, a message to Earth takes up to 22 minutes, and the answer just as long. When something feels wrong, astronauts need help on board first. AURA is health-monitoring software for that gap.

Crew members log blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen, temperature, sleep and mood by hand or from a Smart Watch export, while an Arduino kit watches cabin temperature, humidity and flammable gas. Fixed rules turn the readings into a clear status on an interactive 3D body, flag slow trends before limits are crossed, and give one next step that accounts for the signal delay to Earth. An offline consultation covers 63 conditions, from a possible heart attack to kidney stones in microgravity, and shows the published source behind its guidance. A personal exercise plan targets muscle and bone loss.

NASA data is part of the core: cabin, radiation, sleep, hydration and exercise limits come from NASA Human Research Program pages, OCHMO technical briefs and NASA-STD-3001, and live NASA DONKI and NOAA space-weather data drive a radiation-storm advisory.

No language model makes any health decision. The same tool serves Antarctic station crews and older adults at home. Everyone in the demo is simulated.
details:
Try it: https://auraspace.space/?demo=1 (a guided tour of about three minutes, no account needed, simulated data)

Live app: https://auraspace.space · Code: https://github.com/merenkay/auraspace

WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

AURA helps people check their own health when a doctor is far away: astronauts on a long mission, crews at a polar station and older adults at home. It tracks all six indicators named in the challenge (blood pressure, heart rate, blood sugar, body temperature, sleep and mood) plus blood oxygen, exercise, water and a near-vision check. Readings are entered by hand, imported from a Smart Watch export, or, for the cabin, streamed live from an Arduino sensor kit.

- An interactive 3D anatomy model colours only the body systems that need attention; large tiles show each reading with its status in colour and in words.

- Every alert leads to one next step, and that step depends on the mission: on a Mars transit, where a reply from Earth takes at least six minutes and up to 44, AURA says what to do before the flight surgeon can answer.

- A health score explains itself and refuses to score when there is not enough current data. An early-warning layer flags slow trends against the person's own baseline before a limit is crossed.

- An offline symptom consultation covers 63 conditions. It asks one focused question at a time, treats red-flag combinations as emergencies, says what to do first and what to avoid, checks first-aid medicines against the person's allergies, and shows the published source behind its guidance.

- Symptoms are weighed against the measured cabin air (for example, sweating in a 32 °C cabin), but the environment never lowers an urgent result.

- A personal exercise plan targets muscle and bone loss; daily tasks and a streak prompt regular measurements; a short report goes to the flight surgeon, whose reply returns to the crew member.

- Live NASA DONKI and NOAA space-weather data drive a radiation-storm advisory.

- Experimental hands-free options: a voice assistant that answers questions and can press on-screen controls by name (English and Turkish), and webcam hand-gesture control.

BENEFITS

Help starts on board instead of after a round trip to Earth. The core health rules run in the browser without a connection. Every result is explainable: the same input always gives the same output, and our own modelling choices are labelled "AURA rule". Reports stay short for a low-bandwidth link, and the flight surgeon sees who needs attention first.

INTENDED IMPACT

More autonomy for crews beyond low Earth orbit, where real-time support from Earth is impossible. The same tool fits winter crews at Antarctic stations such as Concordia, isolated for about nine months a year, and older adults at home, where, according to WHO, about 44 % of adults with high blood pressure do not know they have it.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE AND SOFTWARE

TypeScript and React (Vite, Tailwind CSS), three.js for the 3D body and the AURA core, Recharts, the Web Speech API, MediaPipe Hand Landmarker (on the device, input only), Web Serial; PHP 8 and MySQL for accounts, readings and reports; Arduino (C++) with a DHT temperature/humidity sensor and an MQ-2 gas sensor; Vitest with more than 850 automated tests; GitHub Actions and Hostinger. The 3D anatomy is derived from BodyParts3D (CC BY-SA 2.1 JP).

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- Advice that knows how far away help is: the same reading gets a different next step on the ISS, on a Mars transit, at a polar station or at home.

- A medical assistant without a language model: deterministic rules that quote their sources, so every answer can be checked.

- The cabin as part of the patient: environment and symptoms are assessed together, with emergencies never downgraded.

- One system for space and for Earth, and an interface that can be used by voice or by hand gestures when hands are busy.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Safety first: red flags always win, missing or old data never counts as normal, urgent results are never softened.

- Honesty: AURA supports decisions and does not diagnose; it is not clinically validated and not a medical device. Simulated people are labelled. The MQ-2 does not measure carbon monoxide or CO2, NEWS2 is shown as partial, and the radiation dose is a mission-profile model, not a measurement.

- Privacy: each person sees only their own record; mission control never sees mood; demo data stays in the browser.

- Validity: NASA Human Research Program risks, OCHMO technical briefs and NASA-STD-3001 set cabin, radiation, sleep, hydration and exercise limits; clinical guidance comes from public-health sources such as the NHS, CDC and WHO.

- Usability and access: plain language, status shown by colour and word, keyboard and screen-reader support, reduced-motion settings, phone and desktop layouts.

- Limits we know: no testing yet with astronauts, polar crews or older adults, and no clinical review; those are our next steps, together with real device integrations and calibrated sensors.
